flawed_step: After correctly observing that T1 is hereditary, the attempted proof fails when it treats disjoint sets closed in a subspace as though their closures in the ambient normal space were disjoint. Those ambient closures may meet outside the subspace, so ambient normality cannot be applied.
counterexample: Let X=[0,ω₁]×[0,ω] with the product of the ordinal order topologies. Both factors are compact Hausdorff, so X is compact Hausdorff and hence normal and T1. Let Y=X\{(ω₁,ω)}. In Y define A={(ω₁,n):n<ω} and B={(α,ω):α<ω₁}. Their closures in X are respectively A∪{(ω₁,ω)} and B∪{(ω₁,ω)}, so A and B are disjoint closed subsets of Y. Suppose U and V were open subsets of Y containing A and B respectively. For each n<ω, openness of U at (ω₁,n) gives α_n<ω₁ such that (α_n,ω₁]×{n}⊆U. Since {α_n:n<ω} is countable, α*=sup_n α_n<ω₁. Choose γ with α*<γ<ω₁. Since (γ,ω)∈B⊆V, openness of V gives some N<ω such that (γ,n)∈V for every n>N. But γ>α_n for every n, so (γ,n)∈U for every n. Taking n>N yields (γ,n)∈U∩V, a contradiction. Thus Y is not normal although it is a subspace of the normal space X.
assessment_summary: Step 1: the T1 part is inherited by subspaces. Step 2: the separation part cannot be inherited by applying ambient normality, because relative closed sets can acquire a common boundary point outside the subspace. The deleted Tychonoff plank above concretely realizes this obstruction, so normality is not hereditary.
